Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13            Plaintiff sued BB OPCO LLC (“BB OPCO”) and Pichinda Duong in state court for

                                  14   violating California employment laws, and BB OPCO removed to this Court. (Dkt. No. 1.)1 Now

                                  15   pending before the Court is Plaintiff’s motion to remand. (Dkt. No. 12.) Having carefully

                                  16   considered the parties’ submissions, the Court GRANTS Plaintiff’s motion and REMANDS this

                                  17   case to state court. BB OPCO has not shown its second removal is not an improper successive

                                  18   removal or that this Court has subject matter jurisdiction.

                                  19                                            BACKGROUND

                                  20            On February 3, 2026, Plaintiff sued BB OPCO, her former employer, and Ms. Duong, her

                                  21   former supervisor, in Sonoma County Superior Court for violating California labor laws. (Dkt.

                                  22   No. 1-1 at 14-39.) Plaintiff alleges she and Ms. Duong are California residents, and BB OPCO is

                                  23   a limited liability company (“LLC”) registered in California. (Id. at 15.)

                                  24            After it was served on February 24, 2026, (Dkt. No. 1-1 at 2), BB OPCO removed

                                  25   Plaintiff’s case to this Court as Case No. 26-cv-01623-JSC. (Case No. 26-cv-01623-JSC, Dkt. No.

                                  26

                                            Case 3:26-cv-02736-JSC       Document 22        Filed 06/24/26      Page 2 of 10




                                   1   1.) BB OPCO asserted this Court had diversity subject matter jurisdiction because Plaintiff is a

                                   2   California citizen, BB OPCO’s members are not California citizens,2 and Ms. Duong’s citizenship

                                   3   could be disregarded. (Id. at 3-5.) Specifically, BB OPCO did not dispute Ms. Duong is a

                                   4   California citizen but argued (1) “she has not been served as of the date and time of the filing of

                                   5   this Notice of Removal,” and (2) her citizenship “should be disregarded because she is a ‘sham

                                   6   defendant.’” (Id. at 2.)

                                   7            The Court ordered BB OPCO to show cause regarding both removal and subject matter

                                   8   jurisdiction. (Case No. 26-cv-01623-JSC, Dkt. No. 5.) First, the Court noted the “federal removal

                                   9   statute, 28 U.S.C. § 1446, ‘requires all proper defendants to join or consent to the removal

                                  10   notice.’” (Id. at 1 (quoting Prize Frize, Inc. v. Matrix (U.S.) Inc., 167 F.3d 1261, 1266 (9th Cir.

                                  11   1999), superseded by statute on other grounds as stated in Abrego Abrego v. Dow Chem. Co., 443

                                  12   F.3d 676, 681 (9th Cir. 2006).) But BB OPCO’s “Notice of Removal [was] silent as to any efforts
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   made to determine the status of service on Duong and so fail[ed] to adequately explain, as it must,

                                  14   ‘the absence of any co-defendants in the notice of removal.’” (Id. at 2 (quoting Prize Frize, 167

                                  15   F.3d at 1266).) Second, the Court noted BB OPCO’s contention “‘nothing indicates any actions

                                  16   by Duong outside of routine supervisory decisions’” did not “come close to meeting its burden” to

                                  17   show Ms. Duong is a sham defendant. (Id. at 2 (quoting Case No. 26-cv-01623-JSC, Dkt. No. 1 at

                                  18   5).) See Grancare, LLC v. Thrower by & through Mills, 889 F.3d 543, 548 (9th Cir. 2018)

                                  19   (holding the citizenship of a non-diverse defendant can be disregarded only “if a defendant shows

                                  20   that an individual[] joined in the action cannot be liable on any theory” (quotation marks and

                                  21   citation omitted)).

                                  22            In response, BB OPCO first declared it had contacted Ms. Duong prior to removing the

                                  23   case to confirm she had not been served and later learned she had been served two days after BB

                                  24   OPCO’s Notice of Removal. (Case No. 26-cv-01623-JSC, Dkt. No. 6-1 ¶¶ 3-4, Dkt. No. 6-2.) So,

                                  25   the Court held “BB OPCO’s declaration is sufficient to show proper removal” under 28 U.S.C. §

                                       Holdings LLC’s members are California citizens. (Case No. 26-cv-01623-JSC, Dkt. No. 1 at 3.)
                                                                                     2

                                   1   1446, “assuming BB OPCO can secure Ms. Duong’s consent within 30 days from service.” (Case

                                   2   No. 26-cv-01623-JSC, Dkt. No. 7 at 2.) Regarding the Court’s subject matter jurisdiction and

                                   3   whether Ms. Duong is a sham defendant, BB OPCO “withdr[ew] its position that Duong was

                                   4   fraudulently joined.” (Case No. 26-cv-01623-JSC, Dkt. No. 6 at 3 n.2.) The Court therefore held

                                   5   “because BB OPCO has withdrawn its position Ms. Duong was fraudulently joined, and the Court

                                   6   in any event concludes she has not been fraudulently joined under the Ninth Circuit’s binding

                                   7   precedent, Ms. Duong’s citizenship must be considered in determining whether there is complete

                                   8   diversity.” (Case No. 26-cv-01623-JSC, Dkt. No. 7 at 3.) And as BB OPCO did not dispute

                                   9   Plaintiff and Ms. Duong are both California citizens, the Court lacked diversity subject matter

                                  10   jurisdiction; so, on March 12, 2026, remanded the case to state court. (Id.)

                                  11           On March 27, 2026, BB OPCO again removed Plaintiff’s complaint based on diversity

                                  12   jurisdiction. (Dkt. No. 1, Dkt. No. 1-1 at 2, 14-39.) After Plaintiff moved to remand, (Dkt. No.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   12), the case was related to Case No. 26-cv-01623-JSC and assigned to this Court. (Dkt. No. 20.)

                                  14                                             DISCUSSION

                                  15   I.      MOTION TO REMAND
                                  16           In its renewed Notice of Removal, BB OPCO relies on the Court’s prior statement “‘BB

                                  17   OPCO’s declaration is sufficient to show proper removal, assuming BB OPCO can secure Ms.

                                  18   Duong’s consent within 30 days from service.’” (Dkt. No. 1 at 3 (quoting Case No. 26-cv-01623-

                                  19   JSC, Dkt. No. 7 at 2).) So, BB OPCO declares “[o]n March 27, 2026, Duong confirmed her

                                  20   consent to remove this action.” (Dkt. No. 1-1 at 3.) BB OPCO therefore may have met 28 U.S.C.

                                  21   § 1446’s requirement “all defendants who have been properly joined and served must join in or

                                  22   consent to the removal of the action.” 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(2)(A).

                                  23           However, Plaintiff argues for remand because BB OPCO’s Notice of Removal represents

                                  24   an improper successive removal, and BB OPCO has not shown this Court has subject matter

                                  25   jurisdiction.

                                  26           A.      Successive Removal
                                  27           “In general, a party may not file a successive notice of removal on the same grounds where

                                  28   the district court has previously remanded the action.” Wright v. Menzies Aviation, Inc., No. CV
                                                                                        3
                                         Case 3:26-cv-02736-JSC           Document 22           Filed 06/24/26   Page 4 of 10




                                   1   15-05874-RGK (JEMx), 2015 WL 6039238, at *2 (C.D. Cal. Oct. 13, 2015) (citing Seedman v.

                                   2   U.S. Dist. Ct. for Cent. Dist. of Cal., 837 F.2d 413, 414 (9th Cir. 1988) (explaining “a second

                                   3   removal petition based on the same grounds does not ‘reinvest’ the court’s jurisdiction”)).

                                   4   Instead, “[a] successive removal petition is permitted only upon a ‘relevant change of

                                   5   circumstances’—that is, ‘when subsequent pleadings or events reveal a new and different ground

                                   6   for removal.’” Reyes v. Dollar Tree Stores, Inc., 781 F.3d 1185, 1188 (9th Cir. 2015) (quoting

                                   7   Kirkbride v. Cont’l Cas. Co., 933 F.2d 729, 732 (9th Cir. 1991)). “[S]uch changes in

                                   8   circumstances [include], for example, when an intervening change of law gives rise to a new basis

                                   9   for subject-matter jurisdiction . . . [or] when the pleadings are amended to create federal subject-

                                  10   matter jurisdiction for the first time.” Id. (citations omitted).

                                  11           But “where a defendant attempts to remove an action for a second time after conducting its

                                  12   own investigation of the facts, that investigation ‘must be based on newly discovered facts not
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   available at the time of the first removal.’” Lockhart v. Columbia Sportswear Co., No. 5:15-CV-

                                  14   02634-ODW (PLAx), 2016 WL 2743481, at *2 (C.D. Cal. May 11, 2016) (quoting Andersen v.

                                  15   Schwan Food Co., No. EDCV 13-02208 JGB, 2014 WL 1266785, at *4-5 (C.D. Cal. Mar. 26,

                                  16   2014)). So, “consistent with a public policy that ‘guards against premature and protective

                                  17   removals and minimizes the potential for a cottage industry of removal litigation,’ successive

                                  18   removals must be based on new information.” Sweet v. United Parcel Serv., Inc., No. CV09-

                                  19   02653 DDP (RZx), 2009 WL 1664644, at *3 (C.D. Cal. June 15, 2009) (quoting Harris v. Bankers

                                  20   Life & Cas. Co., 425 F.3d 689, 698 (9th Cir. 2005)). Ultimately, “[s]uccessive removals are []

                                  21   improper absent a showing that the posture of the case has so changed that it is substantially a new

                                  22   case.” Wright, 2015 WL 6039238, at *2 (cleaned up); see also Gaus v. Miles, Inc., 980 F.2d 564,

                                  23   566 (9th Cir. 1992) (“The ‘strong presumption’ against removal jurisdiction means that the

                                  24   defendant always has the burden of establishing that removal is proper.” (citations omitted)).

                                  25           BB OPCO has not shown any “relevant change in circumstances . . reveal[s] a new and

                                  26   different ground for removal.” See Reyes, 781 F.3d at 1188 (cleaned up). To the contrary, both of

                                  27   BB OPCO’s Notices of Removals asserted the Court’s subject matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C.

                                  28   § 1332. (Dkt. No. 1-1 at 6; Dkt. No. 1 at 2.) But while BB OPCO’s first Notice of Removal
                                                                                           4
                                         Case 3:26-cv-02736-JSC          Document 22          Filed 06/24/26     Page 5 of 10




                                   1   asserted the Court had had diversity subject matter jurisdiction because Ms. Duong was a sham

                                   2   defendant whose citizenship could be disregarded, (Dkt. No. 1-1 at 6), BB OPCO’s renewed

                                   3   Notice of Removal merely asserts jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a) without further

                                   4   explanation, (Dkt. No. 1 at 2). So, BB OPCO’s renewed Notice of Removal does not show any

                                   5   new or different ground for removal.

                                   6          In opposing Plaintiff’s motion to remand, BB OPCO presents new evidence Ms. Duong

                                   7   lives in California but is a citizen of Thailand rather than the United States. (Dkt. No. 17 at 4; 17-

                                   8   2 ¶ 2.) BB OPCO argues this new evidence serves as a “‘subsequent event[]’ revealing new and

                                   9   different grounds for removal” under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(3) such that its renewed removal is not

                                  10   an improper successive removal. (Dkt. No. 17 at 4-5 (quoting Kirkbride, 933 F.2d at 729).) But

                                  11   rather than present any evidence indicating Ms. Duong’s citizenship status was “not available at

                                  12   the time of [its] first removal,” BB OPCO merely claims it “subsequent[ly] . . . discovered” that
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   fact. (Dkt. No. 17 at 2.) See Lockhart, 2016 WL 2743481, at *2 (“[W]here a defendant attempts

                                  14   to remove an action for a second time after conducting its own investigation of the facts, that

                                  15   investigation ‘must be based on newly discovered facts not available at the time of the first

                                  16   removal.’” (citation omitted)); see, e.g., id. at *3 (allowing removal after deposition testimony

                                  17   revealed for the first time information supporting jurisdiction under the Class Action Fairness

                                  18   Act); Andersen, 2014 WL 1266785, at *5 (rejecting successive removal based on evidence of

                                  19   damages available to the defendants at the time of their first removal, but which the defendants did

                                  20   not investigate until after the first remand). Because BB OPCO has not shown its renewed

                                  21   removal is based on previously unavailable facts, BB OPCO has not shown any “relevant change

                                  22   of circumstances” or “subsequent pleading[] or event[]” justifies its successive removal. See

                                  23   Reyes, 781 F.3d at 1188.

                                  24          Given BB OPCO’s failure to show any relevant change of circumstances, its renewed

                                  25   Notice of Removal is also untimely. Under 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b), after receiving either the initial

                                  26   pleading or “an amended pleading, motion, order, or other paper from which it may first be

                                  27   ascertained that the case is one which is or has become removable,” a defendant has 30 days to file

                                  28   a notice of removal. See 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(1), (3). But BB OPCO was served on February 24,
                                                                                         5
                                         Case 3:26-cv-02736-JSC             Document 22       Filed 06/24/26     Page 6 of 10




                                   1   2026 but did not file the renewed Notice of Removal until March 27, 2026, 31 days after receiving

                                   2   Plaintiff’s complaint. (Dkt. No. 1 ¶ 2.) BB OPCO’s argument its initial Notice of Removal was

                                   3   timely is irrelevant. (Id. ¶ 12.)

                                   4           So, the Court grants Plaintiff’s motion to remand because BB OPCO has not shown its

                                   5   successive removal is not improper or not untimely.

                                   6           B.       Diversity Subject Matter Jurisdiction
                                   7           Furthermore, as the Court explained when remanding Case No. 26-cv-01623-JSC, a

                                   8   removing defendant must also establish federal subject matter jurisdiction. See Canela v. Costco

                                   9   Wholesale Corp., 971 F.3d 845, 849 (9th Cir. 2020). And a case removed to federal court must be

                                  10   remanded to state court “if there is any doubt as to the right of removal in the first instance.” See

                                  11   Grancare, LLC v. Thrower by & through Mills, 889 F.3d 543, 550 (9th Cir. 2018) (quotation

                                  12   marks and citation omitted); see also Valdez v. Allstate Ins. Co., 372 F.3d 1115, 1118 (9th Cir.
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   2004) (explaining a district court should remand if there are doubts regarding its subject matter

                                  14   jurisdiction).

                                  15           Without further explanation, BB OPCO’s Notice of Removal asserts diversity subject

                                  16   matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a), which requires complete diversity of citizenship

                                  17   and an amount in controversy exceeding $75,000. (Dkt. No. 1 at 2.) See 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a). BB

                                  18   OPCO does not reprise its withdrawn argument Ms. Duong is fraudulently joined. Cf. Grancare,

                                  19   889 F.3d at 548 (“In determining whether there is complete diversity, district courts may disregard

                                  20   the citizenship of a non-diverse defendant who has been fraudulently joined.” (citation omitted)).

                                  21   Instead, BB OPCO’s renewed Notice of Removal is silent as to how there is diversity jurisdiction

                                  22   even though its initial Notice of Removal—upon which its renewed Notice of Removal relies to

                                  23   show removal is timely—assumed she was a California citizen but fraudulently joined. (Dkt. No.

                                  24   1-1 at 8.)

                                  25           As explained above, in opposing Plaintiff’s motion to remand, BB OPCO contends for the

                                  26   first time “[a]lthough Duong lives in California, she is not a United States citizen,” and Ms. Doung

                                  27   declares she is instead “a citizen of Thailand.” (Dkt. No. 17 at 4; Dkt. No. 17-2 ¶ 2.) BB OPCO

                                  28   therefore argues the Court has diversity subject matter jurisdiction pursuant to 28 U.S.C. §
                                                                                         6
                                         Case 3:26-cv-02736-JSC           Document 22          Filed 06/24/26      Page 7 of 10




                                   1   1332(a)(3), which provides:

                                   2                  The district courts shall have original jurisdiction of all civil actions
                                                      where the matter in controversy exceeds the sum or value of $75,000,
                                   3                  exclusive of interest and costs, and is between . . . citizens of different
                                                      States and in which citizens or subjects of a foreign state are
                                   4                  additional parties.
                                   5   28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(3). And based on Ms. Duong’s declaration she is a citizen of Thailand, she is

                                   6   a “citizen[] or subject[] of a foreign state.” 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(3).

                                   7          To demonstrate complete diversity for “citizens of different States,” 28 U.S.C. §

                                   8   1332(a)(1), “a party must (a) be a citizen of the United States, and (b) be domiciled in a state of

                                   9   the United States.” Lew v. Moss, 797 F.2d 747, 749 (9th Cir. 1986) (citations omitted). So,

                                  10   although Ms. Duong may be domiciled in California, she is not a citizen of that State because she

                                  11   is not a United States citizen. Furthermore, unlike section 1332(a)(2), which creates an exception

                                  12   for “citizens or subjects of a foreign state who are lawfully admitted for permanent residence in
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   the United States and are domiciled in the same State,” 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(2), “Section

                                  14   1332(a)(3) does not deprive federal courts of jurisdiction over cases involving foreign citizens

                                  15   who are domiciled in the United States.” See Big3 LLC v. Al-Rumaihi, No. CV 18-3466-DMG

                                  16   (SKx), 2018 WL 11470406, at *3 (C.D. Cal. Nov. 29, 2018).

                                  17          Plaintiff’s unsupported argument Ms. Duong is a defendant and therefore not an

                                  18   “additional part[y]” is also unavailing. See 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(3). The Supreme Court has

                                  19   specifically described 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(3) as “confer[ring] jurisdiction in the District Court

                                  20   when a citizen of one State sues both aliens and citizens of a State (or States) different from the

                                  21   plaintiff’s.” See Newman-Green, Inc. v. Alfonzo-Larrain, 490 U.S. 826, 828 (1989); cf. Louisiana

                                  22   Mun. Police Employees’ Ret. Sys. v. Wynn, 829 F.3d 1048, 1056 (9th Cir. 2016) (assuming a

                                  23   defendant could qualify a foreign citizen under 1332(a)(3) but holding the defendant was instead

                                  24   stateless because she was a U.S. citizen domiciled in Macau). So, BB OPCO has shown Ms.

                                  25   Duong is an additional party and citizen of a foreign state.

                                  26          However, section 1332(a)(3) “confer[s] jurisdiction . . . only if there are also diverse U.S.

                                  27   citizens on both sides.” Voltage Pictures, LLC v. Gussi, S.A. de C.V., 92 F.4th 815, 822 (9th Cir.

                                  28   2024), cert. denied, 145 S. Ct. 158 (2024); see also 28 U.S.C § 1332(a)(3) (providing for
                                                                                          7
                                         Case 3:26-cv-02736-JSC          Document 22          Filed 06/24/26    Page 8 of 10




                                   1   jurisdiction in cases between “citizens of different States and in which citizens or subjects of a

                                   2   foreign state are additional parties” (emphasis added)). And as an LLC, BB OPCO “is a citizen of

                                   3   every state in which its owners/members are citizens, not the state in which it was formed or does

                                   4   business.” NewGen, LLC v. Safe Cig, LLC, 840 F.3d 606, 612 (9th Cir. 2016) (quotation marks

                                   5   and citation omitted). But regarding its citizenship, BB OPCO only states:

                                   6                  At the time of filing this action, and at the time of this removal,
                                                      Defendant BB OPCO was and is a Delaware Limited Liability
                                   7                  Company. The only member of Defendant BB OPCO is SPARC
                                                      GROUP BB HOLDINGS LLC. SPARC GROUP BB HOLDINGS
                                   8                  LLC is a Delaware Limited Liability Company. The only member of
                                                      SPARC BB GROUP BB HOLDINGS LLC is SPARC GROUP
                                   9                  HOLDINGS LLC. SPARC GROUP HOLDINGS LLC is a Delaware
                                                      Limited Liability Company. None of the members of SPARC Group
                                  10                  Holdings LLC are citizens of California.
                                  11   (Dkt. No. 17-1 at 23; see also Dkt. No. 17 at 4 (“BB OPCO is not a citizen of California.” (citing

                                  12   Dkt. No. 17-1 at 4)).) So, while BB OPCO presents evidence it is not a citizen of California, it
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   does not show it is a citizen of any U.S. state as it does not allege the citizenship of the members

                                  14   of SPARC Group Holdings LLC, other than that they are not California citizens. BB OPCO has

                                  15   therefore not met its burden to show subject matter jurisdiction under section 1332(a)(3).

                                  16          And although BB OPCO argues its new evidence of Ms. Duong’s citizenship in opposition

                                  17   to Plaintiff’s motion to remand can be treated “as an amendment to its notice of removal,” Cohn v.

                                  18   Petsmart, Inc., 281 F.3d 837, 840 n.1 (9th Cir. 2002) (citing Willingham v. Morgan, 395 U.S. 402,

                                  19   407 n.3 (1969); 28 U.S.C. § 1653), BB OPCO does not provide further explanation regarding its

                                  20   own citizenship.

                                  21   II.    REQUEST FOR FEES AND COSTS
                                  22          Plaintiff also seeks an award of $5,400 in attorneys’ fees, costs, and expenses “incurred as

                                  23   a result of defending against Defendants’ objectively unreasonable re-removal.” (Dkt. No. 12 at 2;

                                  24   see also Dkt. No. 12-1 ¶¶ 7-10 (explaining fees incurred).) District courts have discretion

                                  25   following an order remanding a removed case to state court to “require payment of just costs and

                                  26   any actual expenses, including attorney fees, incurred as a result of the removal.” 28 U.S.C. §

                                  27   1447(c). But “[a]bsent unusual circumstances, courts may award attorney’s fees under § 1447(c)

                                  28   only where the removing party lacked an objectively reasonable basis for seeking removal.”
                                                                                         8
                                         Case 3:26-cv-02736-JSC          Document 22          Filed 06/24/26    Page 9 of 10




                                   1   Lussier v. Dollar Tree Stores, Inc., 518 F.3d 1062, 1065 (9th Cir. 2008) (quoting Martin v.

                                   2   Franklin Cap. Corp., 546 U.S. 132, 141 (2005)). “The appropriate test for awarding fees under §

                                   3   1447(c) should recognize the desire to deter removals sought for the purpose of prolonging

                                   4   litigation and imposing costs on the opposing party, while not undermining Congress’ basic

                                   5   decision to afford defendants a right to remove as a general matter, when the statutory criteria are

                                   6   satisfied.” Martin, 546 U.S. at 140.

                                   7          However, “the burden is on the fee applicant to produce satisfactory evidence—in addition

                                   8   to the attorneys’ own affidavits—that the requested rates are in line with those prevailing in the

                                   9   community for similar services by lawyers of reasonably comparable skill, experience and

                                  10   reputation.” Camancho v. Bridgeport Fin., Inc., 523 F.3d 973, 980 (9th Cir. 2008) (quotation

                                  11   marks and citation omitted). The party requesting fees also bears “the burden of submitting billing

                                  12   records to establish that the number of hours” requested are reasonable. See Gonzalez v. City of
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Maywood, 729 F.3d 1196, 1202 (9th Cir. 2013). Here, in support of its request for attorney’s fees,

                                  14   Plaintiff’s counsel declares its $450 hourly “rate is commensurate with the experience, skill, and

                                  15   the prevailing market rates for attorneys of comparable background handling similar plaintiff-side

                                  16   employment matters in this venue.” (Dkt. No. 12-1 ¶ 7.) And regarding hours, Plaintiff’s counsel

                                  17   explains it “has reasonably expended 7.0 hours to date” and “anticipate[s] expending an additional

                                  18   5.0 hours to bring this Motion to completion.” (Id. ¶¶ 8-9.) Plaintiff does not, however, present

                                  19   further evidence its rates are reasonable or billing records establishing a reasonable number of

                                  20   hours expended.

                                  21          So, regardless of whether BB OPCO’s removal was reasonable, Plaintiff has not met its

                                  22   burden of showing its request for $5,400 in attorney’s fees is reasonable.

                                  23                                             CONCLUSION

                                  24          For the reasons stated above, the Court GRANTS Plaintiff’s motion to remand. The Court

                                  25   again REMANDS this case to the Superior Court of the State of California for the County of

                                  26   Sonoma. The Court further orders that the court file in this case be transferred by the clerk of this

                                  27   Court to the clerk of the State Court, along with a certified copy of this Order of Remand. The

                                  28   State Court may thereupon proceed with this case.
                                                                                         9
                                        Case 3:26-cv-02736-JSC        Document 22       Filed 06/24/26   Page 10 of 10




                                   1          This Order disposes of Docket No. 12.

                                   2          IT IS SO ORDERED.

                                   3   Dated: June 24, 2026
